subject: Cooking
title: Food Trucks: America's Mobile Kitchen Revolution
description: One-minute skill: Food Trucks: America's Mobile Kitchen Revolution.

hook.text: The US food truck industry is worth $1.4 billion. What started as lunch wagons in the 1800s became a culinary movement.

buildup.text: Modern food trucks emerged in 2008 during the recession — chefs couldn't afford restaurants but could afford trucks.

discovery.text: Social media transformed trucks — Twitter and Instagram let chefs announce locations and build loyal followings.

twist.text: Many Michelin-quality chefs now prefer trucks to restaurants — lower overhead, direct customer contact, creative.

climax.text: Cities now have food truck parks — permanent spaces where rotating trucks create ever-changing food halls.

punchline.text: When chefs lost their restaurants, they found something better: wheels.

quiz.question: What economic event sparked the modern food truck movement?

details.summary: Modern food trucks evolved from roach coaches serving construction workers into gourmet mobile kitchens after the 2008 recession when laid-off chefs could not afford restaurant leases.
details.whyItMatters: Food trucks democratized restaurant-quality food by slashing startup costs. They proven that great food does not need a fixed address, only talent and a following.
takeaways: The 2008 recession pushed trained chefs into affordable truck format
Roy Choi's Kogi BBQ pioneered social media-driven food truck culture
Food trucks now generate over $1 billion annually in the United States

faq.question: How did the 2008 recession transform food trucks?
faq.answer: Trained chefs lost restaurant jobs and could not afford traditional leases. Food trucks cost a fraction of brick-and-mortar restaurants. Social media eliminated the need for expensive marketing.

faq.question: What made Roy Choi's Kogi BBQ so revolutionary?
faq.answer: Kogi combined Korean-Mexican fusion with real-time Twitter location updates in 2008. Lines formed around blocks based on tweets alone. It proved that social media could replace traditional restaurant marketing. Kogi showed that food trucks could serve quality comparable to sit-down restaurants.
